title: The Fossil That Was Predicted
standard_text:
Standard: Cite the textual evidence that most strongly supports an analysis of what the text says explicitly as well as inferences drawn from the text.
 Spiral: RI.8.2 central idea · RI.8.3 connections · RI.8.4 word meaning · RI.8.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 870 – 970

paras.label: A
paras.text: Fossils of fish are common in rocks of a certain age, and fossils of four-legged land animals are common in younger rocks. For a long time the interval between them held very little, and that gap was the problem.

paras.label: B
paras.text: A team led by Neil Shubin decided not to search where fossils had already been found. They reasoned instead about where to look, which meant deciding first what kind of rock the animal would have to be in.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The reasoning had three parts. The rock had to date from roughly 375 million years ago, it had to have formed in shallow fresh water rather than deep ocean, and it had to be exposed at the surface rather than buried under a city or a forest.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Very few places satisfy all three. Ellesmere Island, in the Canadian Arctic, does, and the team spent four summers there before finding anything, which is most of the story and the part usually left out.

paras.label: E
paras.text: What they found in 2004 was an animal with the scales and fins of a fish, a flat head with eyes on top, a neck, and inside its fin the bones of a shoulder, an elbow and a wrist.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Several pieces of evidence support the claim that this animal sits between fish and land vertebrates. The anatomy is one. The age of the rock is another. The presence of a neck, which fish do not have, is a third.

paras.label: G
paras.text: But the strongest is the prediction. The anatomy could have been argued over afterwards; what could not be argued over is that the team said what they expected to find, said where, and then went to that place and found it.

Summarize how the team found the fossil and why the find is strong evidence.
questions.a: Rather than searching where fossils were already known, they reasoned that the animal must lie in rock about 375 million years old, formed in shallow fresh water and exposed at the surface, which pointed to Ellesmere Island. questions.q:
vertebrate: an animal with a backbone, which includes both fish and four-legged land animals.
exposed: here, rock lying at the surface where it can be examined, rather than buried under soil or buildings.
Describe the connection between choosing where to dig and the strength of the result.
questions.a: The team said what they expected to find and said where, so going to that place and finding it is evidence that could not be argued over afterwards the way anatomy could.

note: RI.8.1 asks for the evidence that supports a claim most strongly, which means ranking. Paragraph F offers three and paragraph G names a fourth that beats them. Make students defend the order.

title: Who Reached the Pole First
standard_text:
Standard: Cite the textual evidence that most strongly supports an analysis of what the text says explicitly as well as inferences drawn from the text.
 Spiral: RI.8.2 central idea · RI.8.3 connections · RI.8.4 word meaning · RI.8.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 870 – 970

paras.label: A
paras.text: In 1909 two American explorers claimed to have reached the North Pole. Frederick Cook said he had arrived in April 1908, and Robert Peary said he had arrived in April 1909, and each disputed the other.

paras.label: B
paras.text: There is nothing at the Pole to photograph. It is sea ice, indistinguishable from the ice for many kilometres around it, and it drifts, so a party cannot leave a marker and expect anyone to find it again.

paras.label: C
paras.text: That leaves navigation records as the evidence. A traveller establishes position from the height of the sun, measured with a sextant, combined with an accurate time and careful arithmetic recorded as they go.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Cook's case collapsed quickly. His supporting records were thin, and two Inuit companions described a route that did not go far north, and a separate claim he had made about climbing Denali was shown to be false.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Peary's case is argued about still. His party covered distances on the return journey that are difficult to match, and his diary for the days at the Pole is strikingly bare, and he took no navigator with him who could confirm the readings.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Weighing this means ranking kinds of evidence. A diary entry is weaker than a sextant observation, a sextant observation is weaker if nobody independent witnessed it, and a travel speed can be compared against other expeditions.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Most historians now treat the first confirmed surface arrival as a later one. The honest statement is not that Peary lied but that the record he left cannot carry the claim, which is a different and more careful thing to say.

Describe the connection between the absence of an independent navigator and the strength of Peary's claim.
questions.a: A sextant observation is weaker if nobody independent witnessed it, and he took no navigator with him who could confirm the readings.

note: The last sentence models the distinction worth teaching, i.e. a record that cannot carry a claim is not the same as a lie. Students reach for the accusation first.

title: The Bones Inside a Flipper
standard_text:
Standard: Cite the textual evidence that most strongly supports an analysis of what the text says explicitly as well as inferences drawn from the text.
 Spiral: RI.8.2 central idea · RI.8.3 connections · RI.8.4 word meaning · RI.8.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 870 – 970

paras.label: A
paras.text: A whale's flipper is a stiff paddle used for steering. From outside it resembles the fin of a fish, which is unsurprising, because both are solving the same problem in the same medium.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Inside it does not resemble a fin at all. An x-ray shows one long bone, then two bones side by side, then a cluster of small ones, then rows of finger bones, which is the arrangement in a human arm.

paras.label: C
paras.text: A fish fin contains nothing of the kind. It is supported by many thin rays of bone or cartilage, lying parallel to one another and jointed to nothing, and the similarity between a flipper and a fin ends at the skin.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The same arrangement appears in a bat's wing, a horse's leg and a mole's digging hand, and in each the proportions differ enormously while the sequence and the connections stay the same.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Two kinds of evidence are available for the claim that these animals share an ancestor. One is that the limbs look similar from outside. The other is that the bones occur in the same order and the same joints.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The second is far stronger, and the fish fin is why. Outward similarity can be produced by a shared problem, since anything swimming fast will end up streamlined, and a shared problem explains nothing about ancestry.

paras.label: G
paras.text: An arrangement that serves no present purpose is harder to explain away. There is no reason a steering paddle needs finger bones, and the best explanation for their being there is that they were inherited from an animal that used them.

Summarize why the bones inside a flipper are strong evidence of shared ancestry.
questions.a: A flipper looks like a fish fin from outside but contains the same sequence of bones as a human arm, which a fish fin does not have, and the same sequence appears in a bat's wing and a horse's leg. Outward similarity can come from a shared problem such as swimming, so the stronger evidence is an arrangement that serves no present purpose and is best explained as inherited.

questions.q:
streamlined: shaped to move through water or air with little resistance, a form any fast swimmer tends toward.
inherited: passed down from an ancestor, as opposed to developed independently for a present purpose.
Describe the connection between a shared problem and weak evidence of ancestry.
questions.a: Outward similarity can be produced by a shared problem, since anything swimming fast will end up streamlined, and a shared problem explains nothing about ancestry.

note: The ranking is the lesson. Both observations are true and only one is strong, and students who cite the outward resemblance have cited the weaker half.

title: The Shipwreck That Dated a Trade Route
standard_text:
Standard: Cite the textual evidence that most strongly supports an analysis of what the text says explicitly as well as inferences drawn from the text.
 Spiral: RI.8.2 central idea · RI.8.3 connections · RI.8.4 word meaning · RI.8.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 870 – 970

paras.label: A
paras.text: A sponge diver working off the southern coast of Turkey reported metal shapes on the sea floor, described as biscuits with ears. They were copper ingots, and they belonged to a ship that sank around 1300 BCE.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The cargo had not been sorted by a later owner, moved to a museum or rebuilt by anyone. It had gone down in one moment and stayed in position, which makes a wreck a different kind of evidence from a settlement.

paras.label: C
paras.text: What was aboard came from a very wide area. Copper from Cyprus, tin from further east, ebony from Africa, amber from the Baltic, pottery from the Levant, and a gold scarab bearing the name of an Egyptian queen.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Any one of those items could have travelled alone. A single Baltic amber bead in a tomb proves that the bead moved and does not prove that a route existed, because objects can pass through many hands over many years.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Finding them together changes the claim. These goods were in one hold on one voyage, which means a single ship was carrying material from the Baltic and from Egypt at the same time.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The copper and tin matter most of all. They are the two metals bronze is made from, and they occur in very different places, so a bronze age depends on exactly this kind of voyage actually happening.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The strongest evidence here is therefore not the rarest object but the combination. The scarab is the item a museum displays, and the ordinary ingots stacked in rows are the item that proves the route.

note: The closing distinction is the RI.8.1 habit, i.e. the most interesting object and the most probative object are not the same object.

title: What Makes a Fingerprint Evidence
standard_text:
Standard: Cite the textual evidence that most strongly supports an analysis of what the text says explicitly as well as inferences drawn from the text.
 Spiral: RI.8.2 central idea · RI.8.3 connections · RI.8.4 word meaning · RI.8.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 870 – 970

paras.label: A
paras.text: Fingerprint comparison is old, widely used and widely trusted. For most of its history its practitioners described a match as a certainty, and courts accepted that description with very little examination.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The underlying observation is sound. The ridge patterns on a finger form before birth, they are not inherited in detail, and they persist through a lifetime, so two people are very unlikely to share a full print.

paras.label: C
paras.text: What happens in a case is a different operation. A print recovered from a surface is usually partial, smeared, overlapping with others and left in an unknown substance, and it is compared with a clean print taken under controlled conditions.

paras.label: D
paras.text: That comparison is a judgement made by a person. An examiner decides which features count, how many agreements are enough and how to treat a disagreement, and for decades no study measured how often that judgement was wrong.

paras.label: E
paras.text: In 2004 the FBI identified a lawyer in Oregon from a print on a bag connected to the Madrid train bombings. Three examiners agreed. Spanish police matched the same print to someone else, and the identification was withdrawn.

paras.label: F
paras.text: A 2009 report from the National Academies found that the field had not established error rates for most of its methods, and that claims of absolute certainty were not supported by anything that had been measured.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The strongest evidence for a fingerprint method is therefore not how long it has been used or how confident the examiner is. It is a measured error rate from tests where the right answer was known in advance.

In 2004 three FBI examiners matched an Oregon lawyer to a print Spanish police matched to someone else, and a 2009 report found claims of certainty were unsupported, so what counts is a measured error rate.

error rate: how often a method gives the wrong answer, measured on tests where the truth is known.
partial: here, only part of a print, which gives an examiner fewer features to compare.

questions.a: An examiner decides which features count and how many agreements are enough, so until that judgement is tested against known answers there is nothing measuring how often it is wrong.

note: Separate the two claims carefully, i.e. fingerprints are unique and this comparison is correct. The first is well supported and does not establish the second.

title: The Mosquito That Was Engineered
standard_text:
Standard: Determine a central idea of a text and analyze its development over the course of the text, including its relationship to supporting ideas; provide an objective summary of the text.
 Spiral: RI.8.1 citing evidence · RI.8.3 connections · RI.8.5 paragraph structure · RI.8.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 870 – 970

paras.label: A
paras.text: Malaria is carried by a small number of mosquito species, and in much of Africa the main one is Anopheles gambiae. Nets, drugs and spraying have reduced deaths enormously and have not ended the disease, and in some places the mosquitoes have become resistant to the insecticides the nets are treated with.

paras.label: B
paras.text: One proposal is to change the mosquito rather than kill it. A gene can be edited so that females carrying two copies cannot produce eggs, and a population carrying enough of those copies cannot sustain itself.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Ordinary inheritance will not spread such a gene. A harmful variant is passed to about half the offspring and is selected against, so it disappears instead of accumulating.

paras.label: D
paras.text: A gene drive changes that arithmetic. The edited gene carries the machinery to copy itself onto the matching chromosome, so nearly every offspring inherits it, and a variant that reduces fitness can still spread through a population.

paras.label: E
paras.text: In laboratory cages this has worked. Populations collapsed within about ten generations, and the result has been repeated, although a cage is a small, closed, simplified world.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The second idea develops alongside the first. A gene drive is designed to spread, which means it does not respect a national border, and consent for a release is owed to more people than any one government represents.

paras.label: G
paras.text: So the technical question and the governance question cannot be separated. The feature that makes the method work is the same feature that makes it impossible to confine, and a summary that reports only the cage results has reported half of it.

note: RI.8.2 asks how a central idea relates to supporting ideas. Here the second idea is produced by the first rather than added to it, which is the harder relationship to see.

title: The Country That Changed Its Alphabet
standard_text:
Standard: Determine a central idea of a text and analyze its development over the course of the text, including its relationship to supporting ideas; provide an objective summary of the text.
 Spiral: RI.8.1 citing evidence · RI.8.3 connections · RI.8.5 paragraph structure · RI.8.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 870 – 970

paras.label: A
paras.text: In 1928 the Turkish government replaced the Arabic script, which had been used to write Turkish for roughly a thousand years, with a modified Latin alphabet. The change was made law and given a deadline of months.

paras.label: B
paras.text: A linguistic argument was offered. Arabic script marks consonants fully and vowels sparingly, Turkish has eight vowels that matter a great deal, and readers were required to supply from context what the writing did not record.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The new alphabet was designed for the language rather than borrowed whole. Letters were added to carry sounds Turkish has and Latin did not, and the result spells Turkish almost exactly as it is said.

paras.label: D
paras.text: A second argument was political and was stated openly. The new state was turning toward Europe, and a script is visible on every sign, every coin and every document in a way a policy is not.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The cost was immediate and large. Anyone literate in the old script was illiterate in the new one overnight, and material printed before 1928 became unreadable to the generation educated after it.

paras.label: F
paras.text: A nationwide teaching campaign followed, with classes for adults, and literacy rose over the following decades, although separating the effect of the alphabet from the effect of mass schooling is genuinely difficult, since the two arrived together and a child learning to read in 1935 had no earlier script to forget.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The central idea is that a writing system is not only a technology. The practical case and the political case were made at once, and the consequence that an archive became unreadable belonged to both.

questions.a: Arabic script marks consonants fully and vowels sparingly, Turkish has eight vowels that matter a great deal, and readers had to supply from context what the writing did not record.

questions.q: Paragraph D (i.e. the political argument) and paragraph E (i.e. the immediate cost).
Summarize the alphabet change and what it cost.
questions.a: In 1928 Turkey replaced Arabic script with a Latin alphabet designed for the language, arguing that Arabic script recorded Turkish vowels poorly and that a script is visibly European in a way a policy is not. Anyone literate in the old script was illiterate overnight and earlier printing became unreadable, and literacy rose afterwards although mass schooling rose with it.

questions.q:
script: the set of written characters a language is recorded in, as distinct from the language itself.
literate: able to read and write a particular script, which is why a change of script could remove literacy overnight.
Describe the connection between a script being visible and the political argument for changing it.
questions.a: A script is visible on every sign, every coin and every document in a way a policy is not, which is why the turn toward Europe was argued through the alphabet.

note: Ask which of the two arguments the last paragraph says the cost belongs to. The answer is both, and students usually assign it to one.

title: How a Vaccine Stays Cold
standard_text:
Standard: Determine a central idea of a text and analyze its development over the course of the text, including its relationship to supporting ideas; provide an objective summary of the text.
 Spiral: RI.8.1 citing evidence · RI.8.3 connections · RI.8.5 paragraph structure · RI.8.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 870 – 970

paras.label: A
paras.text: A vaccine is a biological product, and biological products degrade with heat. Most routine vaccines must be held between two and eight degrees from the factory to the arm, and some newer ones require storage far colder than any ordinary household freezer can reach.

paras.label: B
paras.text: That requirement produces a system called the cold chain. It includes refrigerated transport, cold rooms at national stores, smaller units at districts and clinics, and insulated carriers for the last stage on a motorcycle or on foot.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The chain fails quietly. A vaccine that has been too warm usually looks exactly the same as one that has not, so a clinic can administer a useless dose and nobody involved will know.

paras.label: D
paras.text: A simple device addresses this. A vial monitor is a small square of heat-sensitive material printed on the label, and it darkens cumulatively with exposure, so a health worker can read the dose's history before using it.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Freezing is the less obvious half of the problem. Several common vaccines are damaged by freezing as surely as by heat, and studies of real supply chains have repeatedly found more exposure to freezing than to overheating.

paras.label: F
paras.text: That turns the goal around. The aim is not to make everything as cold as possible but to hold a range, and a system built only to fight heat will cause the other failure while reporting success.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The central idea is that the hard part is not the refrigerator. It is knowing, at the last clinic in the chain, what has actually happened to the vial in your hand.

title: The Line Drawn in Five Weeks
standard_text:
Standard: Determine a central idea of a text and analyze its development over the course of the text, including its relationship to supporting ideas; provide an objective summary of the text.
 Spiral: RI.8.1 citing evidence · RI.8.3 connections · RI.8.5 paragraph structure · RI.8.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 870 – 970

paras.label: A
paras.text: In July 1947 a British lawyer named Cyril Radcliffe was given the task of drawing the border between India and Pakistan. He had never been to India, and he was given about five weeks.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The brief was to divide two provinces, Punjab and Bengal, by district, taking account of contiguous majority areas and of other factors it did not define. Both provinces had populations living alongside each other everywhere.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The materials were maps and census returns. Radcliffe did not visit the villages, canals or rail junctions he was dividing, and the census categories he worked from had been designed decades earlier for administration rather than for partition, so the counts he relied on had been gathered to answer a different question entirely.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The timetable was not his. Independence had been brought forward, and the award was completed before the date and published two days after it, so people learned which country they were in once both countries existed.

paras.label: E
paras.text: What followed was among the largest forced movements of people in recorded history, with many millions crossing in both directions and very large numbers killed in the violence that accompanied it, often along the same roads, canals and railway lines the new border had cut across.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Assigning responsibility is where accounts diverge. One line of argument places it on the haste and the drafting; another on decisions made years earlier about how communities were counted and represented.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The central idea holds either way. A boundary drawn on a map by a person working from documents becomes, within days, a fact that determines where millions of people may live.

title: The Element That Was Missing
standard_text:
Standard: Determine a central idea of a text and analyze its development over the course of the text, including its relationship to supporting ideas; provide an objective summary of the text.
 Spiral: RI.8.1 citing evidence · RI.8.3 connections · RI.8.5 paragraph structure · RI.8.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 870 – 970

paras.label: A
paras.text: By 1869 chemists knew of around sixty elements and had noticed that some behaved alike. Several people were arranging them in tables, and the arrangements mostly broke down somewhere, usually at a point where an element's weight set it beside elements it had nothing chemically in common with.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Dmitri Mendeleev ordered them by atomic weight and grouped those with similar chemistry. When an element did not fit where the weights put it, he treated that as a problem with the order rather than with the pattern.

paras.label: C
paras.text: His decisive move was to leave gaps. Where the next element along did not have the chemistry the column required, he put an empty space and said an undiscovered element belonged there.

paras.label: D
paras.text: He went further, and this is what separated his table from the others. For three of the gaps he predicted the properties of the missing element: its weight, its density, how its oxide would behave.

paras.label: E
paras.text: In 1875 a French chemist isolated a new element from a zinc ore and named it gallium. Its properties matched one of the predictions closely, except that the measured density was lower than Mendeleev had said.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Mendeleev wrote to suggest the sample was impure and the measurement should be repeated. It was repeated, and the density came out where he had predicted, which is an extraordinary thing for a table to have achieved.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The supporting idea is about what a classification is for. A table that only sorts what is known is a filing system; one that tells you where to look, and what you will find, is doing something else entirely.

title: What an Analogy Costs
standard_text:
Standard: Analyze how a text makes connections among and distinctions between individuals, ideas, or events, for example through comparisons, analogies, or categories.
 Spiral: RI.8.1 citing evidence · RI.8.2 central idea · RI.8.4 word meaning · RI.8.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 870 – 970

paras.label: A
paras.text: An atom is often introduced as a tiny solar system, with a nucleus at the centre and electrons going round it like planets. The picture is memorable, it is easy to draw, and nearly every student meets it first.

paras.label: B
paras.text: It gets several things right. There is a dense centre holding almost all the mass, the rest is mostly empty space, and what is out there is held in place by an attraction toward the middle.

paras.label: C
paras.text: It gets other things wrong in ways that cause trouble later. Electrons do not follow paths, they cannot be assigned a position and a speed at once, and the attraction is electrical rather than gravitational, which behaves differently.

paras.label: D
paras.text: A cell described as a factory has the same shape of problem. The comparison carries the idea of parts with jobs and products moving between them, and it quietly imports a manager, a plan and a purpose.

paras.label: E
paras.text: This is what an analogy does. It transfers a structure from something familiar onto something unfamiliar, and it transfers all of the structure at once, including the parts nobody meant to send and nobody thought to warn about.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The useful habit is to state both halves out loud. Ask what the comparison carries that belongs, and then ask what it carries that does not, because the second list is where misunderstandings are stored.

paras.label: G
paras.text: That does not mean refusing analogies, which would leave most teaching impossible. It means treating an analogy as scaffolding that has to come down, and knowing in advance which parts of it were never the building.

title: The Category Called Teenager
standard_text:
Standard: Analyze how a text makes connections among and distinctions between individuals, ideas, or events, for example through comparisons, analogies, or categories.
 Spiral: RI.8.1 citing evidence · RI.8.2 central idea · RI.8.4 word meaning · RI.8.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 870 – 970

paras.label: A
paras.text: The word teenager is young. It came into common use in the United States in the 1940s, and the stage of life it names is not much older as an idea that anyone organised society around.

paras.label: B
paras.text: For most of history a person moved from childhood to work. The transition was marked by taking on adult labour, and a fourteen-year-old in a mill or on a farm was not in a separate category from the adults beside them.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Three changes built the category. Compulsory schooling held young people in institutions for longer, child labour laws removed them from workplaces, and both together produced a large group of people who were neither children nor workers.

paras.label: D
paras.text: A psychologist named G. Stanley Hall had argued in 1904 that adolescence was a distinct developmental stage with its own characteristics. The claim gave the emerging group a scientific description to be understood through.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Then came the market. Postwar American firms noticed a population with some money, time and no dependants, and products, magazines and music were made specifically for them, which made the category visible to itself.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Once a category exists it generates comparisons. Laws now distinguish by age in dozens of places, from driving to contracts, and each of those lines has to be drawn somewhere even though development does not happen on a birthday.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The useful question is not whether teenagers are real. It is which parts of the category describe something about human development and which parts describe a particular society's schooling, labour laws and shops.

title: Is a Virus Alive?
standard_text:
Standard: Analyze how a text makes connections among and distinctions between individuals, ideas, or events, for example through comparisons, analogies, or categories.
 Spiral: RI.8.1 citing evidence · RI.8.2 central idea · RI.8.4 word meaning · RI.8.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 870 – 970

paras.label: A
paras.text: Biology teaches a list of things living organisms do. They take in energy, they maintain themselves, they respond to their surroundings, they grow and they reproduce, and most examples satisfy all of it comfortably.

paras.label: B
paras.text: A virus satisfies some of it and not the rest. It carries genetic material written in the same chemical alphabet as everything else, it evolves by natural selection, and it reproduces, which is a serious part of the list.

paras.label: C
paras.text: It fails other items outright. A virus has no metabolism, so it takes in no energy and maintains nothing, and outside a host it does not respond to anything or change in any way.

paras.label: D
paras.text: It also cannot reproduce by itself. It carries instructions and no machinery, so it must enter a cell and use that cell's equipment, which means the copying is done by something else.

paras.label: E
paras.text: A tempting response is to say a virus is on the border. That is less useful than it sounds, because a border implies a line already drawn, and the awkwardness is evidence that the line was drawn around familiar examples.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Giant viruses made this worse. Some found since 2003 are larger than small bacteria and carry hundreds of genes, including genes for parts of the machinery viruses were defined as lacking.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The honest conclusion is about categories rather than viruses. Alive is a word that works well for the cases it was built from, and a case it handles badly is telling you about the word, not reporting a mystery about the thing.

title: What Counts as a City
standard_text:
Standard: Analyze how a text makes connections among and distinctions between individuals, ideas, or events, for example through comparisons, analogies, or categories.
 Spiral: RI.8.1 citing evidence · RI.8.2 central idea · RI.8.4 word meaning · RI.8.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 870 – 970

paras.label: A
paras.text: Comparing two cities by population sounds like a simple lookup. It is not, because the number depends entirely on which of several boundaries somebody used, and there are at least three in ordinary use that disagree with one another.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The first is the administrative boundary, the line a government draws for the purpose of governing. It is the one that appears on an official document, and it was often drawn long ago and seldom moved since.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The second is the built-up area, defined by where the buildings actually are. It ignores administration completely, and it can be much larger or much smaller than the city as a government defines it.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The third is the commuting area, defined by where the people who work in a place live. It is usually the largest of the three, and it is the one that matches how a region functions day to day.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The choice changes answers dramatically. A city with a tightly drawn old boundary and a vast surrounding region will look modest by the first measure and very large by the third, with the same people in the same houses.

paras.label: F
paras.text: This is not an obscure technicality. Rankings of the world's largest cities disagree with one another for exactly this reason, and funding, representation and planning decisions follow whichever definition a document uses.

paras.label: G
paras.text: So the first question to ask of any city figure is which boundary produced it. Two numbers that disagree are often not in conflict at all, because they are answers to two different questions.

paras.text: The third is the commuting area, defined by where the people who work there live. It is usually the largest. It matches how a region actually functions each day.

paras.text: The choice changes answers a lot. A city with a tight old boundary and a huge surrounding region looks modest by the first measure and very large by the third. Same people, same houses.

paras.label: F
paras.text: This is not an obscure technicality. Rankings of the world's largest cities disagree for exactly this reason. Funding, representation and planning follow whichever definition a document uses.

paras.label: G
paras.text: So ask first which boundary produced a figure. Two numbers that disagree are often not in conflict. They are answers to two different questions.

questions.q: What are the three boundaries a city population can be measured against?
questions.a: The administrative boundary a government draws, the built-up area defined by where the buildings are, and the commuting area defined by where the people who work there live.

questions.q: Paragraph E (i.e. how the choice changes the answer) and paragraph G (i.e. why two disagreeing numbers may not conflict).
Summarize why city populations are hard to compare.
questions.a: A population figure depends on whether it uses the administrative boundary, the built-up area or the commuting area, and a city with a tight old boundary looks modest by the first and very large by the third with the same people in the same houses. Rankings disagree for this reason, and funding and planning follow whichever definition a document uses.

questions.q:
administrative boundary: the line a government draws for the purpose of governing, which may not match where the buildings are.
commuting area: the region from which people travel in to work, usually the largest of the three definitions.
Describe the connection between the definition used and decisions about funding.
questions.a: Funding, representation and planning decisions follow whichever definition a document uses, so the choice of boundary is not only a measurement question.

note: The closing move is the one to practise, i.e. deciding whether two figures conflict or answer different questions. It recurs at RI.8.9.

title: Why a Peanut Is Not a Nut
standard_text:
Standard: Analyze how a text makes connections among and distinctions between individuals, ideas, or events, for example through comparisons, analogies, or categories.
 Spiral: RI.8.1 citing evidence · RI.8.2 central idea · RI.8.4 word meaning · RI.8.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 870 – 970

paras.label: A
paras.text: A peanut is not a nut, an almond is not a nut, and a cashew is not a nut. Each of those statements is true in botany and useless in a kitchen, which is the interesting part.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Botanically a true nut is a hard, dry fruit that does not split open to release its seed. A hazelnut, an acorn and a chestnut qualify, and almost nothing else people call a nut does.

paras.label: C
paras.text: A peanut is a legume. It grows in a pod, in the same family as peas and beans, and it ripens underground, which is a fairly loud signal that it is not doing what a hazel tree does.

paras.label: D
paras.text: An almond is the seed inside a drupe, a fleshy fruit with a stone, which makes it a relative of a peach. A cashew is also a seed, attached outside a fruit, which is stranger than either.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Cooking uses a different category altogether, and it is a perfectly good one. A nut in a kitchen is something hard, oily, high in fat and used in the ways those things are used, and that grouping predicts how an ingredient will behave.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Medicine uses a third. Allergy guidance separates peanuts from tree nuts, because the proteins differ and a person allergic to one may safely eat the other, which neither of the first two categories captures.

paras.label: G
paras.text: None of the three is wrong. They are built for different purposes, and the mistake is only ever expecting a category assembled to answer one question to answer a different one correctly.

title: Calling It a Greenhouse
standard_text:
Standard: Determine the meaning of words and phrases as they are used in a text, including figurative, connotative, and technical meanings; analyze the impact of specific word choices on meaning and tone, including analogies or allusions to other texts.
 Spiral: RI.8.1 citing evidence · RI.8.3 connections · RI.8.6 point of view · RI.8.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 870 – 970

paras.label: A
paras.text: The warming effect of certain gases in the atmosphere is called the greenhouse effect, and the comparison is now so standard that almost nobody checks whether a greenhouse works the way the name suggests.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The explanation usually offered is that glass lets sunlight in and stops heat escaping. Light passes through, warms what is inside, and the warmth is then trapped by the glass, which is why the air in there gets hot.

paras.label: C
paras.text: That is not mainly what a greenhouse does. Its chief effect is to stop air moving. Warm air inside cannot rise away and be replaced by cool air from outside, and preventing that exchange does most of the heating.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The atmosphere does something genuinely different. Certain gases are transparent to incoming sunlight and absorb the infrared radiation the warmed surface sends back out, then re-emit it in all directions, including downward.

paras.label: E
paras.text: So the mechanisms do not match. One works by blocking the movement of air and the other by absorbing and re-emitting radiation, and a student who reasons carefully from the greenhouse will reach a wrong conclusion.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The name has stuck anyway, and it has done real work. It gave a difficult idea a handle that a person could carry, and almost everyone now knows the phrase, which cannot be said of radiative forcing.

paras.label: G
paras.text: That is the trade an analogy makes in a name. It buys recognition with accuracy, and the cost does not fall at the moment of naming but later, on the student who takes the comparison seriously and follows it.

title: The Allusion in a Speech
standard_text:
Standard: Determine the meaning of words and phrases as they are used in a text, including figurative, connotative, and technical meanings; analyze the impact of specific word choices on meaning and tone, including analogies or allusions to other texts.
 Spiral: RI.8.1 citing evidence · RI.8.3 connections · RI.8.6 point of view · RI.8.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 870 – 970

paras.label: A
paras.text: A speech can borrow authority without quoting anything. A phrase shaped like an older text brings the older text with it, and listeners who recognise the shape supply what is not said.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Lincoln opened at Gettysburg with four score and seven years ago. He could have said eighty-seven. The older construction puts the sentence in the register of scripture and of formal public address rather than of arithmetic.

paras.label: C
paras.text: That is one function of an allusion, which is to set a tone. The second is to place a claim inside an argument that an audience already accepts, so the new claim arrives with support it did not have to earn in the room.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The same address then dates the nation from 1776 rather than from the Constitution. That is not a flourish. It is a choice about which founding document the war was being fought to defend, made in the first sentence.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Allusion carries a risk that quotation does not. A listener who does not recognise the source loses the layer entirely, and may hear only an odd phrasing, so an allusion divides an audience in a way a quotation does not.

paras.label: F
paras.text: It is also deniable. A speaker who alludes has not said the thing, so the reference can be insisted on by those who hear it and denied by the speaker, and both can point at the same words.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Reading for allusion therefore means reading for what is almost there. The question is not only what the sentence says but what older sentence it is standing near, and what that neighbour is being asked to lend it.

note: RI.8.4 adds allusion to the grade 7 standard. Paragraph F is the part students find most useful outside English class.

title: The Genome Is Not a Blueprint
standard_text:
Standard: Determine the meaning of words and phrases as they are used in a text, including figurative, connotative, and technical meanings; analyze the impact of specific word choices on meaning and tone, including analogies or allusions to other texts.
 Spiral: RI.8.1 citing evidence · RI.8.3 connections · RI.8.6 point of view · RI.8.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 870 – 970

paras.label: A
paras.text: A genome is often called a blueprint for an organism. The comparison is everywhere, it has been in textbooks for decades, and it gets the most important thing backwards.

paras.label: B
paras.text: A blueprint is a scaled drawing. Every line on it corresponds to a part of the finished building, the drawing can be measured, and a person can point at a door on the plan and at the same door in the corridor.

paras.label: C
paras.text: A genome does not work that way. There is no region you can point to that corresponds to a hand, and no part of it is a picture of anything; what it holds are instructions for making molecules that interact.

paras.label: D
paras.text: A recipe is closer, though not perfect. A recipe is a sequence of operations rather than a picture of a cake, you cannot point to the part of it that is the crust, and the result depends on conditions during the process.

paras.label: E
paras.text: That difference carries consequences. Blueprint language suggests a fixed plan being executed, which makes it sound as though a trait is simply read out, and it makes environment sound like interference with a plan.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Development is not interference. Temperature decides the sex of some reptiles, nutrition changes which genes are active, and the same genome run twice does not produce identical organisms, which a blueprint implies it would.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The word choice therefore shapes what people think is possible. Blueprint invites the question of what a gene is for; recipe invites the question of what happens under which conditions, and only one of those questions has answers.

title: Naming a Disease
standard_text:
Standard: Determine the meaning of words and phrases as they are used in a text, including figurative, connotative, and technical meanings; analyze the impact of specific word choices on meaning and tone, including analogies or allusions to other texts.
 Spiral: RI.8.1 citing evidence · RI.8.3 connections · RI.8.6 point of view · RI.8.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 870 – 970

paras.label: A
paras.text: Diseases used to be named after wherever they were first noticed, whoever described them, or whatever animal they were associated with. Each of those conventions has produced a name that caused harm, and in several cases the harm fell on people who had nothing to do with the outbreak.

paras.label: B
paras.text: A place name attaches a population to an illness. The influenza pandemic of 1918 is still widely called Spanish flu, and Spain's association with it comes mainly from Spain being neutral and not censoring its press.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The consequences are not confined to feelings. Names referring to animals or foods have been followed by collapses in unrelated trade, and names referring to places have been followed by harassment of people from them.

paras.label: D
paras.text: In 2015 the World Health Organization published guidance. New disease names should avoid geographic locations, people's names, animal species, references to culture or occupation, and words that provoke undue fear.

paras.label: E
paras.text: What is recommended instead is descriptive and dull: the symptoms, the affected system, the pathogen, with a year or an identifier where one is needed. The resulting names are harder to remember, which is partly the point.

paras.label: F
paras.text: A dull name is also harder to campaign with, and that cuts both ways. It denies a slogan to people who would use a vivid one badly, and it gives public health communicators nothing memorable to work with either.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The guidance is about consequence rather than offence. A name travels further and faster than any correction to it, so the choice made in the first week determines what a population is called for a century.

title: What a Chemist Means by Organic
standard_text:
Standard: Determine the meaning of words and phrases as they are used in a text, including figurative, connotative, and technical meanings; analyze the impact of specific word choices on meaning and tone, including analogies or allusions to other texts.
 Spiral: RI.8.1 citing evidence · RI.8.3 connections · RI.8.6 point of view · RI.8.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 870 – 970

paras.label: A
paras.text: Organic is a word with two confident meanings that have almost nothing to do with each other. Both are correct, both are used daily, and the overlap between the people using each one is large enough to cause regular confusion.

paras.label: B
paras.text: In a supermarket it describes how food was produced. It refers to a set of rules about what may be applied to a crop or given to an animal, and a certificate and an inspection stand behind it.

paras.label: C
paras.text: In chemistry it describes what a compound is made of. Organic chemistry is the chemistry of carbon compounds, and a substance is organic if it contains carbon in the relevant arrangements, whatever its origin.

paras.label: D
paras.text: By that definition petrol is organic, most plastics are organic, and so is every pesticide built on a carbon skeleton, which is a sentence that sounds like a trick and is simply the technical meaning applied consistently.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The older sense explains how this happened. Chemists once believed compounds from living things required a vital force and could not be made from non-living material, so organic meant from an organism.

paras.label: F
paras.text: That belief did not survive the laboratory. In 1828 Friedrich Wöhler made urea, a compound from living organisms, out of starting materials that were not, and the boundary the word described turned out not to exist.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The word stayed where the boundary had been. A technical term can outlive its own justification, and when it does, it keeps a shape that no longer matches anything, which is exactly when an everyday meaning moves in beside it.

title: How a Paragraph Builds a Definition
standard_text:
Standard: Analyze in detail the structure of a specific paragraph in a text, including the role of particular sentences in developing and refining a key concept.
 Spiral: RI.8.2 central idea · RI.8.3 connections · RI.8.6 point of view · RI.8.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 870 – 970

paras.label: A
paras.text: Take a paragraph defining the word species in a biology textbook and read it one sentence at a time. The paragraph is short, and almost every sentence in it is doing a different job from the one before.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The first sentence usually offers the definition plainly: a species is a group of organisms that can interbreed and produce fertile offspring. On its own that sentence sounds complete, which is the effect it is written to have.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The second sentence almost always narrows it. It adds a condition such as under natural conditions, which excludes animals that will breed only in captivity, and the definition is now smaller than it was a sentence ago.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The third sentence tends to introduce the trouble. Bacteria do not interbreed at all, many plants hybridise freely across what everyone calls species, and fossils cannot be tested for anything of the kind.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The fourth does repair work. It either admits that the definition covers some organisms and not others, or it introduces a second definition used where the first fails, and either move changes the status of sentence one.

paras.label: F
paras.text: So the opening sentence is not the definition the paragraph delivers. It is a first approximation the rest of the paragraph edits, and a reader who stops after it has the version the author already decided was insufficient.

paras.label: G
paras.text: This shape is everywhere in technical writing. Claim, narrow, complicate, repair, and the sentence most often quoted elsewhere is the first one, which is the only sentence in the paragraph the author did not mean to stand alone.

paras.label: A
paras.text: Take a paragraph defining the word species in a biology textbook. Read it one sentence at a time. The paragraph is short. Almost every sentence does a different job from the one before.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The first sentence usually gives the definition plainly. A species is a group that can interbreed and produce fertile offspring. On its own it sounds complete. It is written to sound that way.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The second sentence almost always narrows it. It adds a condition like under natural conditions. That excludes animals that breed only in captivity. The definition is now smaller.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The third sentence brings the trouble. Bacteria do not interbreed at all. Many plants hybridise across what everyone calls species. Fossils cannot be tested for any of this.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The fourth repairs. It admits the definition covers some organisms and not others. Or it adds a second definition for where the first fails. Either move changes the first sentence.

paras.label: F
paras.text: So the opening sentence is not the definition the paragraph delivers. It is a first try that the rest edits. A reader who stops there has the version the author already called insufficient.

paras.label: G
paras.text: This shape is everywhere in technical writing. Claim, narrow, complicate, repair. The sentence quoted elsewhere is usually the first, the only one not meant to stand alone.

questions.q: What job does the second sentence of such a paragraph usually do?
questions.a: It narrows the definition by adding a condition such as under natural conditions, which excludes animals that will breed only in captivity.

questions.q: Paragraph E (i.e. the repair sentence) and paragraph F (i.e. why the opening sentence is not the definition).
Summarize the four jobs the sentences of a definition paragraph do.
questions.a: The first states the definition plainly so it sounds complete, the second narrows it with a condition, the third introduces cases it fails on such as bacteria and fossils, and the fourth repairs by admitting a limit or adding a second definition. The opening sentence is a first approximation the rest of the paragraph edits.

questions.q:
hybridise: to breed across what are normally treated as separate species and produce offspring.
approximation: a first version that is close enough to begin with and is expected to be corrected.
Describe the connection between quoting the first sentence and misrepresenting the paragraph.
questions.a: The first sentence is the one the rest of the paragraph edits, so a reader who stops after it has the version the author already decided was insufficient.

note: RI.8.5 is about one paragraph. Give students a definition paragraph with the sentences numbered and ask them to label each with claim, narrow, complicate or repair.

title: The Sentence That Concedes
standard_text:
Standard: Analyze in detail the structure of a specific paragraph in a text, including the role of particular sentences in developing and refining a key concept.
 Spiral: RI.8.2 central idea · RI.8.3 connections · RI.8.6 point of view · RI.8.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 870 – 970

paras.label: A
paras.text: In the middle of a well-made argument there is usually a sentence that appears to work against it. It grants something to the other side, and it is placed deliberately rather than let in by accident.

paras.label: B
paras.text: It is easy to spot once you look. It begins with although, admittedly, it is true that, or of course, and whatever follows is a point the writer is not disputing and does not intend to come back and dispute later.

paras.label: C
paras.text: A reader might expect such a sentence to weaken the paragraph. It generally strengthens it, because an argument that never grants anything signals either that the writer has not met the objections or has decided not to mention them.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The sentence after a concession is where the work happens. It usually begins with but, yet or however, and it does not deny what was just granted; it argues that the granted point does not reach the conclusion.

paras.label: E
paras.text: That pairing is what makes a concession safe to make. The writer accepts a fact and then disputes its weight, and a reader who understands that structure will not mistake the concession for a change of mind.

paras.label: F
paras.text: A concession can also be used badly. A writer may grant a small point while leaving the serious objection unmentioned, which produces the appearance of fairness at a very low price.

paras.label: G
paras.text: So the test is what gets conceded, not whether anything does. Find the strongest objection you can think of and ask whether the paragraph names it, because a concession that avoids the hard one is a performance.

Granting nothing suggests the writer has not met the objections, but granting only a small point while leaving the serious one unmentioned produces the appearance of fairness cheaply.

concession: a sentence granting a point to the opposing side within one's own argument.
weight: how much a granted fact actually supports a conclusion, which is what the following sentence disputes.

questions.a: A writer may grant a small point while leaving the serious objection unmentioned, so the test is to find the strongest objection and ask whether the paragraph names it.

note: This is the structural half of RI.8.6, taught a standard early. Students who can find the concession can usually find the author's position straight afterwards.

title: The Paragraph That Reports Nothing Happened
standard_text:
Standard: Analyze in detail the structure of a specific paragraph in a text, including the role of particular sentences in developing and refining a key concept.
 Spiral: RI.8.2 central idea · RI.8.3 connections · RI.8.6 point of view · RI.8.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 870 – 970

paras.label: A
paras.text: A result that shows no effect is harder to write up than one that shows an effect, and it is harder to publish, and for a long time most of them were never written up at all.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The paragraph reporting such a result has an unusual job. It has to establish that the study could have found an effect if one had been there, because otherwise the finding is indistinguishable from having run a poor experiment.

paras.label: C
paras.text: So it opens by stating what was measured and how precisely. A confidence interval appears early, and a narrow interval around zero says something quite different from a wide one that includes large effects in both directions.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The next sentences describe the study's power, which is the chance it had of detecting an effect of a given size. A study with low power that finds nothing has found nothing about the world.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Only then does the paragraph state the result, and careful writing states it as a bound rather than as an absence. The phrasing is not we found no effect but any effect is smaller than this.

paras.label: F
paras.text: That distinction matters more than it looks. An absence is unprovable, a bound is a measurement, and the second can be combined with other studies while the first cannot be combined with anything.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Such paragraphs are now easier to find because trials are registered before they run, so a study that reports nothing can be matched against the plan it was registered with, and one that is never reported leaves a visible gap.

power: the chance a study had of detecting an effect of a given size if one existed.

title: The Definitions Section of a Law
standard_text:
Standard: Analyze in detail the structure of a specific paragraph in a text, including the role of particular sentences in developing and refining a key concept.
 Spiral: RI.8.2 central idea · RI.8.3 connections · RI.8.6 point of view · RI.8.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 870 – 970

paras.label: A
paras.text: Many laws open with a section that does nothing but define words. It is skipped by almost every reader, including many who are otherwise reading carefully, and it frequently determines the outcome of every dispute the law produces.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The convention is a single paragraph built from repeated clauses: in this Act, vehicle means, employee means, premises means. The repetition is deliberate, because a definition that varies in form invites argument about whether the variation meant something.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Each clause is doing one of two opposite jobs. Some widen an ordinary word so it covers more than usual, and some narrow it so a familiar word excludes cases a reader would assume were included.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The widening clauses are the ones to watch. A definition saying vehicle includes any device for carrying a person by land is reaching for things nobody would call a vehicle in conversation, and that reach is the law's actual scope.

paras.label: E
paras.text: There is usually a sentence near the end doing something different again. It says that where a word is not defined here it carries its ordinary meaning, which quietly puts a dictionary into the statute.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The order within the paragraph matters too. A term used inside another definition has to be defined before or alongside it, so the sequence often reveals which concept the drafters treated as basic.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Reading this section first changes the rest. A sentence later in the law that looked clear often turns out to be using at least one word in a sense that was fixed in a paragraph the reader skipped.

questions.a: Some widen an ordinary word so it covers more than usual, and some narrow it so a familiar word excludes cases a reader would assume were included.

questions.q: Paragraph E (i.e. the sentence about undefined words) and paragraph F (i.e. what the order of definitions reveals).
Summarize what a definitions section does and why it should be read first.
questions.a: It defines words in repeated clauses, each either widening an ordinary word beyond normal use or narrowing it to exclude cases a reader would assume, with a closing sentence giving undefined words their ordinary meaning. The order shows which concepts the drafters treated as basic, and a later sentence that looks clear may use a word in a sense fixed here.

questions.q:
statute: a written law passed by a legislature.
scope: how far a law reaches, which the widening definitions establish rather than the later sentences.
Describe the connection between skipping the definitions and misreading a later sentence.
questions.a: A sentence later in the law that looked clear often turns out to be using at least one word in a sense that was fixed in the paragraph the reader skipped.

note: Bring one real definitions section. Ask which clauses widen and which narrow, then ask what the law would cover without them.

title: One Paragraph of a Forecast Discussion
standard_text:
Standard: Analyze in detail the structure of a specific paragraph in a text, including the role of particular sentences in developing and refining a key concept.
 Spiral: RI.8.2 central idea · RI.8.3 connections · RI.8.6 point of view · RI.8.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 870 – 970

paras.label: A
paras.text: Behind the icons on a weather app there is a document most people never see. Forecasters write a discussion in prose, for other forecasters, explaining how they reached the forecast and where they are unsure.

paras.label: B
paras.text: A paragraph from one of these has a recognisable structure. It opens with the current situation, states what the computer models are showing, notes where the models disagree, and then gives the forecaster's judgement between them.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The disagreement sentence is the most informative one in the paragraph. Two models placing a low pressure system a hundred kilometres apart produce very different weather for a particular town, and the public forecast cannot show that.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Next comes the reasoning. A forecaster may prefer one model because it has handled this pattern well this season, or because its starting conditions used observations the other one lacked, and the preference is stated with its reason.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Confidence is given explicitly and in words. A paragraph will say high confidence in the timing and low confidence in the amount, which separates two things that a single percentage on a screen merges into one.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The last sentences usually say what would change the forecast. If the overnight model run shifts the track west, the whole picture changes, and naming that in advance is a commitment rather than a hedge.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The app shows a cloud with a number under it. The same forecast in prose shows the uncertainty, the disagreement, the reason for a choice, and the observation that would overturn it, which is four things the icon cannot carry.

model: a computer simulation of the atmosphere, several of which may disagree about the same day.
confidence: here, how sure a forecaster is about a particular element, stated separately for timing and amount.

questions.a: Saying in advance that an overnight shift in the track would change the whole picture is a commitment rather than a hedge, because it states beforehand what would overturn the forecast.

note: Pull a real discussion from a weather service and read one paragraph aloud. Students can usually label all five moves on a second reading.

title: The Paper That Answers Its Critics
standard_text:
Standard: Determine an author's point of view or purpose in a text and analyze how the author acknowledges and responds to conflicting evidence or viewpoints.
 Spiral: RI.8.1 citing evidence · RI.8.4 word meaning · RI.8.8 claims and evidence · RI.8.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 870 – 970

paras.label: A
paras.text: A scientific journal does not only print papers. It prints comments on papers, and replies to those comments, and the whole exchange is published under the names of the people having it, in the same volume as the work being argued about.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The sequence is fixed. Someone publishes a result, another researcher writes a comment arguing it is wrong, the original authors reply, and all three appear in the record where anyone can read them together.

paras.label: C
paras.text: What a comment does is narrower than disagreement. It identifies a specific step: an analysis that should have excluded certain data, a control that was missing, an alternative explanation the paper did not rule out.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The reply is the interesting document, because a reply has only a few honest moves available. The authors can show the step was handled and say where, they can accept the point and state what survives it, or they can present new analysis.

paras.label: E
paras.text: What a reply cannot do is ignore the objection and restate the original claim more firmly. Readers can see both texts at once, and a reply that does not engage is visible as such immediately.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The exchange also fixes a date. After a published comment, the objection is on the record, so later work that repeats the original claim without addressing it is making a choice rather than an oversight.

paras.label: G
paras.text: This is why a field's disagreements are worth reading rather than avoiding. A paper on its own shows what its authors concluded; a paper with its comment and reply shows what the authors could defend when someone pushed.

A reply can show the step was handled, accept the point and say what survives, or present new analysis, but cannot ignore the objection, and after a published comment later work repeating the claim is making a choice.

questions.a: Readers can see both texts at once, so a reply that does not engage with the objection is visible as such immediately.

title: The Report With a Minority View
standard_text:
Standard: Determine an author's point of view or purpose in a text and analyze how the author acknowledges and responds to conflicting evidence or viewpoints.
 Spiral: RI.8.1 citing evidence · RI.8.4 word meaning · RI.8.8 claims and evidence · RI.8.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 870 – 970

paras.label: A
paras.text: When a committee is asked to investigate something, it is usually expected to agree. A single report carries more weight than several competing ones, and the people who appointed the committee generally want one answer they can act on.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Sometimes a member will not sign. The usual mechanism is a separate statement printed inside the same report, placed after the main findings and labelled as a minority or dissenting view.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The placement is the point. Printing the disagreement inside the document means a reader of the report cannot avoid knowing that it exists, which would not be true if the member had resigned and written elsewhere.

paras.label: D
paras.text: A good minority statement is narrow. It does not restate the whole investigation; it names the findings it accepts, identifies the one or two it does not, and says what evidence it thinks was weighed wrongly.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The majority then has a decision to make. Some reports respond to the dissent directly in the main text, which strengthens both documents, and some leave it standing unanswered, which tells a reader something as well.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Minority statements have a particular history of being right. A dissent that was ignored at the time is sometimes the part of a report still being quoted decades later, usually after the thing it warned about happened.

paras.label: G
paras.text: That is not an argument that dissents are usually correct, because most are not. It is an argument for printing them, since a report that shows its disagreement lets a later reader check who had seen what.

title: The Review That Weighs Studies
standard_text:
Standard: Determine an author's point of view or purpose in a text and analyze how the author acknowledges and responds to conflicting evidence or viewpoints.
 Spiral: RI.8.1 citing evidence · RI.8.4 word meaning · RI.8.8 claims and evidence · RI.8.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 870 – 970

paras.label: A
paras.text: On most questions in medicine there is not one study but dozens, and they do not all agree. A systematic review is the document written to deal with that, and its method is as important as its conclusion.

paras.label: B
paras.text: It begins before any results are looked at. The authors write down what question they are asking, which studies will count, and how the studies will be assessed, and they publish that plan in advance.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The order protects against a specific failure. An author who reads the studies first and then writes the inclusion rules can produce any answer they want, simply by setting a boundary that excludes the inconvenient ones.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The search is then meant to be exhaustive rather than convenient. Reviewers search several databases, look for unpublished work, and write down how many studies they found and how many they excluded at each stage, with reasons.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Each included study is assessed for risk of bias. A trial where participants knew which group they were in is not weighted the same as one where nobody did, and the assessment is reported study by study rather than averaged away.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Only then are results combined, and sometimes they should not be. If the studies measured different things in different populations, a single pooled number hides the disagreement instead of resolving it, and a careful review says so.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The conclusion of such a review carries weight because of everything that came before it. A review that announces its answer without showing the plan, the search and the assessment is an opinion with a bibliography.

paras.label: A
paras.text: On most questions in medicine there is not one study but dozens. They do not all agree. A systematic review deals with that. Its method matters as much as its conclusion.

paras.label: B
paras.text: It begins before any results are seen. The authors write down the question, which studies will count, and how studies will be assessed. They publish that plan in advance.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The order protects against a specific failure. An author who reads the studies first and then writes the rules can produce any answer. They set a boundary that excludes the inconvenient ones.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The search is meant to be exhaustive, not convenient. Reviewers search several databases and look for unpublished work. They record how many studies they found and excluded, with reasons.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Each included study is assessed for risk of bias. A trial where participants knew their group is not weighted like one where nobody did. The assessment is reported study by study.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Only then are results combined, and sometimes they should not be. If studies measured different things in different populations, one pooled number hides the disagreement. A careful review says so.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The conclusion carries weight because of what came before it. A review that announces an answer without showing the plan, the search and the assessment is an opinion with a bibliography.

questions.q: Why is the plan published before the results are examined?
questions.a: An author who reads the studies first and then writes the inclusion rules can produce any answer they want by setting a boundary that excludes the inconvenient studies.

questions.q: Paragraph E (i.e. assessing risk of bias study by study) and paragraph F (i.e. when results should not be combined).
Summarize what a systematic review does.
questions.a: It writes down the question, the inclusion rules and the assessment method before looking at results, searches exhaustively and records what was excluded and why, assesses each study for risk of bias separately, and only then combines results, saying so when studies measured different things in different populations and should not be pooled.

questions.q:
systematic review: a review that states its method in advance and applies it to every study it finds.
risk of bias: the ways a study's design could have pushed its result in a particular direction.
Describe the connection between the method and the weight of the conclusion.
questions.a: The conclusion carries weight because of the plan, the search and the assessment that came before it, and a review without those is an opinion with a bibliography.

note: This is how a field answers conflicting evidence at scale. Pair it with The Paper That Answers Its Critics, which is the same job for one disagreement.

title: The Textbook That Shows Two Views
standard_text:
Standard: Determine an author's point of view or purpose in a text and analyze how the author acknowledges and responds to conflicting evidence or viewpoints.
 Spiral: RI.8.1 citing evidence · RI.8.4 word meaning · RI.8.8 claims and evidence · RI.8.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 870 – 970

paras.label: A
paras.text: A history textbook has to decide what to do when historians disagree, and on a great many topics they do. The easy option is to pick one account and tell it plainly, and most textbooks written for younger readers do exactly that.

paras.label: B
paras.text: There are reasons for it. A reader who does not yet know the basic events cannot evaluate a dispute about them, and a book that opens every topic with a controversy can leave a student unable to say what happened.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The cost appears later. A student taught one account with no sign that there was ever an argument will read a second account as an error, and will have no practice at the thing historians actually do.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Some textbooks handle it by setting two short passages side by side with their sources named, and asking what each emphasises. The arrangement is honest about there being a choice to make.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Done badly it becomes a habit of its own. Presenting every question as two balanced views implies the evidence is always evenly divided, and on many questions it is not, which is its own kind of distortion.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The better versions distinguish the cases. Some disagreements are about what the evidence shows, some are about which evidence matters, and some are between a position with substantial support and one with very little.

paras.label: G
paras.text: What a reader can do is check whether a book ever says historians disagree. A textbook that never does is making a claim about its field, and the claim is almost certainly false.

title: The Scientist Who Published a Correction
standard_text:
Standard: Determine an author's point of view or purpose in a text and analyze how the author acknowledges and responds to conflicting evidence or viewpoints.
 Spiral: RI.8.1 citing evidence · RI.8.4 word meaning · RI.8.8 claims and evidence · RI.8.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 870 – 970

paras.label: A
paras.text: Published research is sometimes wrong, and the system has two formal ways of saying so. A correction fixes an error while leaving the conclusion standing, and a retraction withdraws the paper entirely.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The distinction is about reach. A mislabelled axis or a wrong sample size in a table is corrected; an error that undermines the result, or evidence that the data were not what they were said to be, produces a retraction.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Both are published rather than quietly applied. The original paper stays in the record with a notice attached, because papers that have already been cited cannot be removed from the work that cited them.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Authors do not always initiate these. Some corrections follow an outside reader finding the problem, and some retractions are issued by a journal over the authors' objection, and the notice usually says which happened.

paras.label: E
paras.text: That makes the wording of a notice worth reading. A notice saying the authors identified an error and reported it describes a different event from one saying the journal was unable to obtain the original data.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The incentives run against admitting anything. A correction is a public statement that a published result was wrong, and the people best placed to find an error are the authors, who have the least to gain from finding it.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Which is why the researchers who correct their own work are worth noticing. The number of corrections a field publishes is not a measure of how often it is wrong; it is a measure of how often it says so.

title: Why Every Flat Map Is Wrong
standard_text:
Standard: Evaluate the advantages and disadvantages of using different mediums, for example print or digital text, video or multimedia, to present a particular topic or idea.
 Spiral: RI.8.1 citing evidence · RI.8.2 central idea · RI.8.9 conflicting texts · RI.8.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 870 – 970

paras.label: A
paras.text: A globe shows the earth accurately and is almost useless. It cannot be folded, carried in a pocket, printed in a book or displayed on a screen, and a flat map can do all of those things and cannot be accurate.

paras.label: B
paras.text: This is not a failure of effort. A sphere cannot be flattened without stretching, and that is a proved result in geometry rather than a practical limitation that better techniques might remove.

paras.label: C
paras.text: So every projection chooses what to preserve. Mercator keeps angles correct, which is why a compass bearing is a straight line on it, and the price is area: Greenland appears comparable to Africa and is about a fourteenth of its size.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Equal-area projections make the opposite trade. They show the relative sizes of landmasses correctly and distort shape instead, so continents appear stretched, and they are unusable for the navigation Mercator was built for.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The choice therefore depends on the job. A sailor and a person comparing the land area of countries need different maps, and arguing about which projection is correct without naming a purpose is arguing about nothing.

paras.label: F
paras.text: A globe, a flat map and an interactive map that reprojects as you move each fail differently. The globe cannot show the whole surface at once, the flat map distorts, and the interactive one shows no overview at all.

paras.label: G
paras.text: What a reader can do is look for the projection's name, usually printed small at an edge. A map that does not say which projection it uses has withheld the one fact needed to know what it is distorting.
