title: The Archive on Paper and on a Server
standard_text:
Standard: Evaluate the advantages and disadvantages of using different mediums, for example print or digital text, video or multimedia, to present a particular topic or idea.
 Spiral: RI.8.1 citing evidence · RI.8.2 central idea · RI.8.9 conflicting texts · RI.8.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 870 – 970

paras.label: A
paras.text: A letter written on good paper and kept dry can be read in five hundred years by anyone who knows the language, with no equipment at all and no intervening effort. That is an unusual property, and it is worth stating plainly before discussing anything digital.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Digital storage is better at almost everything else. A server holds a collection in a fraction of the space, serves it to anyone anywhere, and lets a reader search a million pages for a phrase in under a second.

paras.label: C
paras.text: It is worse at lasting. Storage media degrade within decades, and more importantly formats stop being readable, so a file saved in a word processor from thirty years ago may now require software nobody distributes.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The response is active rather than passive. Digital preservation means copying collections to new media and migrating them to current formats on a schedule, which is a continuing cost rather than a one-off purchase.

paras.label: E
paras.text: That changes what an archive is. A paper archive survives neglect for a long time and is destroyed by fire or flood; a digital archive survives fire easily and is destroyed by twenty years of nobody paying the bill.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The failures are also differently visible. A damaged page announces itself, while a corrupted file may open and display what looks like the document with a section silently missing.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Serious archives therefore use both. The original is kept because it is the thing itself and degrades slowly, and the scan is kept because it can be read, searched and copied, and neither substitutes for the other.

title: The Diagram and the Equation
standard_text:
Standard: Evaluate the advantages and disadvantages of using different mediums, for example print or digital text, video or multimedia, to present a particular topic or idea.
 Spiral: RI.8.1 citing evidence · RI.8.2 central idea · RI.8.9 conflicting texts · RI.8.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 870 – 970

paras.label: A
paras.text: A physics problem about a block on a slope can be given two ways. One is a diagram with arrows on it. The other is a set of equations, and both describe exactly the same situation.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The diagram is better at the first step. It shows how many forces there are, roughly which way each points, and which ones must balance, and a mistake like forgetting friction is visible as a missing arrow.

paras.label: C
paras.text: It is worse at the second step. A diagram cannot be solved. Arrows do not combine, an angle drawn by hand is not a measured angle, and a picture does not say what happens when the slope gets steeper.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The equations do what the diagram cannot. They can be rearranged, combined and taken to a limit, and the same expression that answers this problem answers every problem of the same shape.

paras.label: E
paras.text: They are worse at catching a missing term. An equation with a force left out still looks like an equation, it still solves, and it returns an answer that is wrong without looking wrong.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Which is why physicists teach the diagram first and then do not throw it away. The picture is where the model gets checked, and the symbols are where it gets solved, and a student using only one of them fails in a predictable direction.

paras.label: G
paras.text: This is a general point about mediums rather than a point about physics. Each one makes a particular kind of error easy to see, and switching between them is how the errors each one hides get caught.

title: The Museum Case and the Scan
standard_text:
Standard: Evaluate the advantages and disadvantages of using different mediums, for example print or digital text, video or multimedia, to present a particular topic or idea.

paras.label: A
paras.text: An object in a museum case is the thing itself. It has a size a visitor can stand next to, a surface that catches light, and a presence that comes partly from knowing it is not a copy.

paras.label: B
paras.text: It is also almost unreachable. It can be seen from one side, at one distance, in one building, by whoever can travel there, and it cannot be handled, turned over or looked at from underneath.

paras.label: C
paras.text: A high-resolution scan reverses nearly all of that. It can be rotated, enlarged, measured, lit from any angle, examined by a researcher on another continent, and handed to a class in a school with no museum nearby.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The scan also supports work the object cannot. Measurements can be taken from it without touching anything, tool marks can be exaggerated with artificial lighting, and a fragment can be compared with a fragment held elsewhere.

paras.label: E
paras.text: What it loses is scale and material. A screen gives no sense of mass, a surface rendered smoothly loses the roughness a hand would feel, and nothing in a file tells a viewer that an object is heavy.

paras.label: F
paras.text: There is also the question of what a scan is of. A scan is a measurement made at a moment with a particular instrument, so it records the object as it is now, including damage, restoration and the decisions of whoever did the scanning.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Treating the two as alternatives is the error. A scan does not replace an object any more than a photograph of a person replaces them, and an object in a case does not give a researcher the measurements they need.

title: The Photograph That Is Not a Photograph
standard_text:
Standard: Evaluate the advantages and disadvantages of using different mediums, for example print or digital text, video or multimedia, to present a particular topic or idea.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A famous image of a nebula looks like a photograph of something a traveller could fly past and see. It is not, and almost everything that makes it striking is a decision rather than an observation.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The telescope did not record colour. It recorded brightness through a series of narrow filters, each admitting light of one particular wavelength, and each exposure came back as a grey image.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Those filters are usually chosen for chemistry rather than appearance. One admits the light emitted by hydrogen, another by oxygen, another by sulphur, so each grey frame is a map of where one element is.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The colour image is built by assigning each frame to red, green or blue and combining them. The assignment is a choice, and a different assignment of the same data produces an image with completely different colours.

paras.text: The trouble is what happens to the image afterwards. It is reproduced without its caption, and a reader who meets it on a screen has no way of knowing that the colours encode elements rather than appearance.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The medium is doing the work here. A labelled diagram of the same data would be read as an interpretation, and the same information in the form of a photograph is read as a view, because that is what photographs usually are.

title: Does the Full Moon Change Behaviour?
standard_text:
Standard: Delineate and evaluate the argument and specific claims in a text, assessing whether the reasoning is sound and the evidence is relevant and sufficient; recognize when irrelevant evidence is introduced.
 Spiral: RI.8.1 citing evidence · RI.8.5 paragraph structure · RI.8.6 point of view · RI.8.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 870 – 970

paras.label: A
paras.text: The belief that a full moon changes human behaviour is widespread and old. Nurses, police officers and teachers report busier nights, and the reports are sincere, numerous and offered as evidence.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Testing it is straightforward, because the moon's phase is known in advance for every date in history. Researchers can take years of records and compare the nights without deciding anything after the fact.

paras.label: C
paras.text: This has been done many times with births, emergency admissions, crimes and calls to police lines. Reviews gathering those studies together have repeatedly found no consistent effect.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The reports are still worth explaining rather than dismissing. A busy night followed by someone saying it must be a full moon creates a memory that joins the two; a busy night with no moon mentioned creates no such memory.

paras.label: E
paras.text: That is a mechanism, and it predicts what should be found: the belief should be strongest among people who work nights, which it is, and the effect should vanish when records are counted, which it does.

paras.label: F
paras.text: A particular kind of argument is often offered in reply. The moon moves the tides, people are mostly water, so the moon must move something in a person, and the reasoning is confident and has nothing to do with the question.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Tides are produced by the difference in pull across an ocean-sized object. A person is not large enough for that difference to amount to anything, and in any case an effect this would predict would show up in the records, which it does not.

title: The Petition With a Thousand Signatures
standard_text:
Standard: Delineate and evaluate the argument and specific claims in a text, assessing whether the reasoning is sound and the evidence is relevant and sufficient; recognize when irrelevant evidence is introduced.
 Spiral: RI.8.1 citing evidence · RI.8.5 paragraph structure · RI.8.6 point of view · RI.8.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 870 – 970

paras.label: A
paras.text: A petition arrives at a council meeting with a thousand signatures asking that a road be closed to through traffic. The number is read out at the start, before anything else in the document is described, and it is treated as the strongest part of the case.

paras.label: B
paras.text: For some questions it genuinely is. If the question is whether residents want the road closed, a thousand signatures is direct evidence about what residents want, which is the thing being asked.

paras.label: C
paras.text: For other questions it is no evidence at all. If the claim is that closing the road will reduce accidents, the number of people who believe that has no bearing on whether it is true.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Mixing the two is where petitions go wrong. A document that says a thousand residents agree the closure will improve safety is offering a count of opinions in the place where a traffic study belongs.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The reverse error is just as common. A council that dismisses a petition because signatures are not data has dismissed real evidence about preference, which is one of the things a council is supposed to weigh.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Some additional questions sharpen it. How many signatories live on the road, how were they asked, and what did the sheet they signed actually say, because a petition is also a survey with no controls.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The habit worth building is to split the document. Mark every sentence that reports what people want and every sentence that claims what will happen, and then ask whether the signatures support the second kind.

title: The Testimonial in a Health Claim
standard_text:
Standard: Delineate and evaluate the argument and specific claims in a text, assessing whether the reasoning is sound and the evidence is relevant and sufficient; recognize when irrelevant evidence is introduced.
 Spiral: RI.8.1 citing evidence · RI.8.5 paragraph structure · RI.8.6 point of view · RI.8.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 870 – 970

paras.label: A
paras.text: An advertisement for a supplement carries a photograph and a quotation. Someone describes the pain they had for years, the product they took, and how much better they feel now, and the account is specific, detailed and convincing in a way a statistic is not.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The first thing to notice is that it may well be true. Treating a testimonial as a lie misses the point, because the problems with it survive the account being completely honest.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Most conditions vary. People seek a remedy when symptoms are at their worst, and symptoms at their worst tend to improve afterwards whatever is done, which produces a real recovery with no cause attached.

paras.label: D
paras.text: There is also a selection problem. The advertisement contains the people who improved, and the people who took the product and felt nothing were not photographed and did not send a quotation.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Both of these are why trials use a comparison group. Half receive the product and half do not, neither group knows which, and the question becomes whether the first group improved more than the second.

paras.label: F
paras.text: A testimonial cannot do that arithmetic even in principle. It is one person, with no comparison group and no record of what would have happened otherwise, selected for inclusion precisely because of the outcome, and adding nine more testimonials produces ten of the same thing rather than evidence.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Watch for the sentence that follows. Advertisements often pair a testimonial with a phrase such as studies suggest, which borrows the authority of research for a claim the testimonial above it cannot support.

title: The Argument That Changes the Subject
standard_text:
Standard: Delineate and evaluate the argument and specific claims in a text, assessing whether the reasoning is sound and the evidence is relevant and sufficient; recognize when irrelevant evidence is introduced.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A council is debating whether to put a bus lane on a main road. One speaker argues that the lane will slow deliveries, and a second rises to say that the first speaker does not even live in the district.

paras.label: B
paras.text: That may be true and it is not a reply. The claim on the table is about deliveries, and whether it is correct does not depend in any way on where the person making it sleeps.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Dealing with the speaker rather than the claim is the oldest move in the catalogue. It works because an audience that has lost confidence in a person stops examining what the person said, which is the effect it is produced for.

paras.label: D
paras.text: A related move answers a different question than the one asked. Asked whether the lane will slow deliveries, a supporter who replies that the road has needed investment for years has said something true and answered nothing.

paras.label: E
paras.text: A third version raises the stakes until the question disappears. If the debate becomes whether a speaker is against public transport in general, the specific question about delivery times has quietly left the room.

paras.label: F
paras.text: These are hard to catch in the moment because they feel like continuations. Each new sentence follows the one before it, and the drift away from the question happens one reasonable-sounding step at a time.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The defence is to write the question down. Keep the sentence that was actually asked in front of you and check each contribution against it, because a contribution that does not touch it is not part of the argument.

title: The Chart With a Cut Axis
standard_text:

paras.label: A
paras.text: A bar chart shows two columns, and the second is visibly twice the height of the first. The impression is immediate, and it is produced by the drawing rather than by the numbers.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The key is at the bottom left. The vertical axis does not start at zero; it starts at a value chosen to sit just below the smaller bar, so the part shown is only the top slice of each column.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The effect is dramatic. Two values of 48 and 52 drawn from zero look almost identical, and drawn from 47 one looks twice the other, with the same two numbers printed above them in both versions.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Cutting an axis is not automatically dishonest. On a line chart tracking a quantity that never goes near zero, such as body temperature, starting at zero wastes the whole chart on empty space and hides the variation that matters.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The rule that actually works is about what the shape encodes. A bar says compare these lengths, so a bar chart must start at zero, and a line says watch this move, so a line may legitimately start anywhere.

paras.label: F
paras.text: There are other versions of the same trick. A second axis with a different scale, a time range beginning at a convenient year, and unequal spacing along the bottom all change a shape without touching a number.

paras.label: G
paras.text: So the first thing to read on any chart is the axes, before the shape. The shape is the part that persuades, and it is produced by decisions that are printed in small type at the edges.

title: Two Inquiries Into One Disaster
standard_text:
Standard: Analyze a case in which two or more texts provide conflicting information on the same topic and identify where the texts disagree on matters of fact or interpretation.

paras.label: A
paras.text: The space shuttle Challenger broke apart in January 1986, shortly after launch, killing all seven aboard. A presidential commission was appointed, and it produced a report within months.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The commission established the immediate cause without serious dispute. A rubber seal in a joint of a solid rocket booster failed to close the joint at the unusually low temperature on the morning of the launch.

paras.label: C
paras.text: On that point there is no conflict between the texts. The physical finding was agreed by everyone, demonstrated in a public hearing with a piece of the material and a glass of iced water, and it has never been contested.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The conflict is about the second question, which is how the decision to launch was made. The main report describes a flawed decision-making process, and it is written in the measured language of an official document.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Richard Feynman, a member of the commission, did not think the main report said what the evidence showed. His own analysis was published as an appendix, separately, after he made clear he would not otherwise sign.

paras.label: F
paras.text: That appendix reports that management put the chance of a catastrophic failure at about one in a hundred thousand while engineers working on the same hardware put it nearer one in a hundred, and it calls the gap a failure of the organisation rather than of a process.

paras.label: G
paras.text: So the two texts agree entirely about the seal and disagree about what the seal demonstrates. One is a disagreement about fact and there is none here; the other is about interpretation, and that is where the whole dispute sits.

paras.text: After a large public gathering, two numbers appear. The organisers give one figure, the authorities give another, and the two often differ by a factor of three or more for the same afternoon in the same square.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Neither side has to be lying for this to happen. Counting a crowd is a measurement problem, and a figure depends on decisions that are rarely stated: which area was counted, at what time, and what density was assumed.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The standard method multiplies area by density. A photograph taken from above is divided into zones, a density is estimated for each, and the total depends heavily on whether a zone is judged to hold one person per square metre or four.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Time is the second variable. A march passes a point over several hours, so a count at the densest moment and a count of everyone who attended at any point are different quantities, and both can be called the size of the crowd.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Area is the third. Including the side streets and the park at the edge can double a figure, and a photograph taken from one end makes a judgement about the boundary that the caption rarely records.

paras.label: F
paras.text: So the first question is not who is right but what each number measures. Two figures three times apart may both be accurate answers to questions that differ in area, in timing and in assumed density.

paras.label: G
paras.text: This is a disagreement about fact rather than interpretation, which is what makes it solvable. Publishing the photograph, the zone boundaries and the densities used turns an argument about numbers into an argument about method, which can be settled.

title: Two Studies That Disagree About Coffee
standard_text:
Standard: Analyze a case in which two or more texts provide conflicting information on the same topic and identify where the texts disagree on matters of fact or interpretation.
 Spiral: RI.8.2 central idea · RI.8.6 point of view · RI.8.8 claims and evidence · RI.8.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 870 – 970

paras.label: A
paras.text: One study reports that coffee drinkers live longer. Another reports no benefit. Both are published, both are large, and both were conducted by competent researchers who are not disputing each other's honesty.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Neither assigned anyone to drink coffee. Both followed groups of people who had already made that choice, recorded what happened over years, and compared the groups, which is the only practical design for a question like this.

paras.label: C
paras.text: That design has a known weakness. People who drink coffee differ from people who do not in many other ways, and some of those ways affect health directly, so a difference in outcome may belong to something else entirely.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Researchers adjust for the differences they can measure. One study may adjust for smoking, income and exercise, and another for those plus diet and existing illness, and the two will then report different numbers from similar data.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The definitions differ too. One study's heavy drinker is four cups a day and another's is two, the populations are from different countries with different drinking habits, and the follow-up periods are different lengths.

paras.label: F
paras.text: So where do they actually disagree? Rarely about a fact. The underlying observations are usually compatible, and the conflict is in interpretation: which adjustments were appropriate and how much a remaining difference should be trusted.

paras.label: G
paras.text: This is why a single nutrition study is almost never worth changing anything for. The useful document is the review that reads a field's studies together and reports where their methods differ, which is where the conflict actually lives.

title: Two Maps of the Same War
standard_text:
Standard: Analyze a case in which two or more texts provide conflicting information on the same topic and identify where the texts disagree on matters of fact or interpretation.
 Spiral: RI.8.2 central idea · RI.8.6 point of view · RI.8.8 claims and evidence · RI.8.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 870 – 970

paras.label: A
paras.text: Two newspapers print a map of the same conflict on the same day. The front lines are drawn in different places, the shaded areas differ, and some towns appear on one map and not the other.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Some of that is genuine disagreement about fact. Who holds a particular town on a particular morning may be unknown, disputed on the ground, or changing hourly, and two sources with different contacts will say different things.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Much of it is not about facts at all. A map has to decide what counts as holding territory, and a force present on a road in daylight and absent at night is treated as holding it by one convention and not by another.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Shading makes this worse. A solid colour over a district implies uniform control, and a situation where a government holds the towns and someone else moves freely between them cannot be drawn that way honestly.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Names carry a position too. A town with two names in two languages has to be labelled somehow, and whichever is chosen is read by someone as a claim, including when the mapmaker meant only to be understood.

paras.label: F
paras.text: What is omitted is hardest to see. A map showing only the front line and not the refugee movements, or only territory and not who controls the electricity, has chosen a subject as much as a style.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Comparing two maps therefore means asking three questions in order. Where do they disagree about who holds what, where do they use different definitions of holding, and what has each chosen not to put on the page at all?

paras.label: A
paras.text: Two newspapers print a map of the same conflict on the same day. The front lines sit in different places. The shaded areas differ. Some towns appear on one map and not the other.

questions.a: Some differences are genuine disagreements about who holds a town on a given morning, but a map must also define what holding means, and solid shading implies uniform control that may not exist. Names carry claims and omissions are hardest to see, so comparing two maps means asking where they disagree on fact, where they define holding differently, and what each left out.

convention: an agreed rule for representing something, such as what counts as holding territory.
omission: what a map leaves out, which shapes the reader's understanding without appearing on the page.

note: The three questions in paragraph G are the standard restated as a procedure. They work on any two documents, not only maps.

title: Two Dates for the Same Site
standard_text:
Standard: Analyze a case in which two or more texts provide conflicting information on the same topic and identify where the texts disagree on matters of fact or interpretation.
 Spiral: RI.8.2 central idea · RI.8.6 point of view · RI.8.8 claims and evidence · RI.8.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 870 – 970

paras.label: A
paras.text: An archaeological site is excavated and two dates are published for the same layer. One comes from radiocarbon measurement of charcoal, and the other from the position of the layer within the sequence of deposits above and below it.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The methods answer slightly different questions. Radiocarbon dates the death of the organism the sample came from, and stratigraphy dates the layer relative to the layers around it, so the two are not measuring the same event.

paras.label: C
paras.text: That gap explains a classic conflict. A piece of charcoal from long-dead wood can be older than the fire it was burned in, so a radiocarbon date may be genuinely correct and still predate the human activity it is being used to date.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Material can also move. Burrowing animals, roots and later digging carry small objects downward through a sequence, so a sample can be recovered from a layer it was not deposited in and date that layer wrongly.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Calibration adds a further step. Radiocarbon years are not calendar years, and converting between them uses a curve built from tree rings, which has flat stretches where a single measurement corresponds to a range of several centuries.

paras.label: F
paras.text: So the first question when two dates conflict is what each one dated. A disagreement between the death of a tree and the position of a layer is not a disagreement about when people were there.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Where that does not resolve it, the conflict is real and is usually settled by more samples. Several dates from several materials in several layers constrain a sequence in a way one measurement from one piece of charcoal never can.

title: The Experiment That Weighed the Earth
standard_text:
Standard: By the end of the year, read and comprehend literary nonfiction at the high end of the grades 6-8 text complexity band independently and proficiently.
 Spiral: RI.8.1 citing evidence · RI.8.2 central idea · RI.8.4 word meaning · RI.8.8 claims and evidence
 Lower range: LL 870 – 970

paras.label: A
paras.text: In 1798 Henry Cavendish published a measurement of the density of the earth. He did it in a shed in his garden, with two lead spheres, two smaller ones, a wooden rod and a wire.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Gravity between everyday objects is extraordinarily weak. Two lead balls on a table attract each other with a force far too small to feel, and the problem was not understanding the effect but detecting it at all.

paras.label: C
paras.text: His apparatus turned a tiny force into a visible rotation. A rod with a small lead ball at each end hung horizontally from a thin wire, and twisting the wire even slightly required almost no force.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Two large spheres were then brought up beside the small ones. Their attraction swung the rod, the wire twisted, and the angle of the twist gave the size of the force, since the stiffness of the wire had been measured beforehand.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The hard part was everything else. A person in the room warms one side of the air, a draught moves the rod more than gravity does, so Cavendish observed through a telescope from outside and worked the apparatus with pulleys.

paras.label: F
paras.text: From the force he obtained the density of the earth, about five and a half times that of water, which is more than any surface rock and was the first real evidence of a dense metallic interior.

paras.label: G
paras.text: His result stood for a century within about one per cent. The experiment is still run in teaching laboratories today, and students using modern equipment in a climate-controlled building rarely do much better.

title: The City That Reversed Its River
standard_text:
Standard: By the end of the year, read and comprehend literary nonfiction at the high end of the grades 6-8 text complexity band independently and proficiently.
 Spiral: RI.8.1 citing evidence · RI.8.2 central idea · RI.8.4 word meaning · RI.8.8 claims and evidence
 Lower range: LL 870 – 970

paras.label: A
paras.text: Chicago grew beside a lake it drank from and a river it used as a drain. The river ran into the lake, which meant the city's sewage arrived back at the intake pipes that supplied its drinking water.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The consequences were measured in outbreaks. Typhoid and cholera moved through the city repeatedly through the nineteenth century, and extending the water intake further out into the lake bought time rather than a solution.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The solution adopted was to make the river run the other way. A canal was cut from the river toward the Des Plaines, deep enough that water would flow away from the lake and toward the Mississippi watershed.

paras.label: D
paras.text: It worked, in the sense that the engineering did what it was designed to do. The river reversed in 1900, the intake pipes stopped receiving the city's own waste, and deaths from waterborne disease in Chicago fell sharply.

paras.label: E
paras.text: It also moved the problem downstream. The state of Missouri sued, arguing that Chicago was sending its sewage toward St Louis, and the case went to the Supreme Court, which did not stop the canal.

paras.label: F
paras.text: There were effects nobody litigated. The canal connected two watersheds that had been separate, and species have since moved between them in both directions, which is a consequence still being managed today.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The story is usually told as engineering triumph or as environmental warning. It is more useful as neither, since what it actually shows is a real problem genuinely solved by an action whose consequences were larger than the problem.

title: The Bacteria That Eat Rock
standard_text:
Standard: By the end of the year, read and comprehend literary nonfiction at the high end of the grades 6-8 text complexity band independently and proficiently.
 Spiral: RI.8.1 citing evidence · RI.8.2 central idea · RI.8.4 word meaning · RI.8.8 claims and evidence
 Lower range: LL 870 – 970

paras.label: A
paras.text: Almost every familiar food chain starts with sunlight. Plants capture it, animals eat the plants, other animals eat those, and tracing any meal backwards far enough arrives at a leaf and then at the sun.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Some organisms do not begin there. Certain bacteria obtain energy by driving chemical reactions on minerals, taking electrons from iron or sulphur compounds in rock, and they require no light at any stage.

paras.label: C
paras.text: They live where that chemistry is available, which turns out to be a very large volume. They have been recovered from boreholes kilometres deep, from the rock beneath the ocean floor, and from water that has been isolated underground for a long time.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Life down there runs slowly. Estimates of generation times in some deep communities run to centuries rather than hours, which is difficult to study because an experiment outlasts the researcher by a wide margin.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The total is genuinely uncertain and genuinely large. Published estimates put a substantial fraction of all bacterial cells on earth below the surface, and the range between the low and high estimates is itself wider than most ecosystems.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The finding matters beyond the organisms. It means energy and carbon move through rock in ways geology alone does not describe, and that some mineral deposits have had biological help in forming.

paras.label: G
paras.text: It also changes a question. If life does not require a star's light but only a source of chemical energy and liquid water, then the places worth examining for it are not limited to the surfaces of planets.

generation time: how long an organism takes to reproduce, which in some deep communities is estimated in centuries.
Describe the connection between not needing light and where life might be found.
questions.a: If life does not require a star's light but only a source of chemical energy and liquid water, the places worth examining for it are not limited to the surfaces of planets.

note: Paragraph E is honest about a wide uncertainty without abandoning the claim, which is the habit grade 8 has been building since RI.8.1.

title: The Day the Clocks Were Standardised
standard_text:
Standard: By the end of the year, read and comprehend literary nonfiction at the high end of the grades 6-8 text complexity band independently and proficiently.
 Spiral: RI.8.1 citing evidence · RI.8.2 central idea · RI.8.4 word meaning · RI.8.8 claims and evidence
 Lower range: LL 870 – 970

paras.label: A
paras.text: For most of history every town kept its own time. Noon was when the sun stood highest over that town, so clocks in two places a hundred kilometres apart genuinely disagreed, and nothing was wrong with either.

paras.label: B
paras.text: This caused no difficulty while travel was slow. A journey taking two days absorbed a few minutes of difference without anyone noticing, and local time was both accurate and sufficient.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Railways removed that tolerance. A timetable has to state a departure time, and a train crossing many towns in an afternoon cannot leave at a different noon in each, so railway companies began publishing their own time.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The result was worse than either system alone. A station could be running on railway time while the town outside ran on local time, so the clock on the platform and the clock on the church disagreed by minutes that mattered.

paras.label: E
paras.text: In November 1883 the railway companies of North America adopted a shared scheme of time zones. Within each zone every clock read the same, and the boundaries were drawn where the companies found them convenient.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Governments followed rather than led. An international conference the following year fixed a prime meridian for the purpose of reckoning longitude and time, and national legislation in many countries came later still.

paras.label: G
paras.text: So a unit everyone treats as natural was settled by companies with a scheduling problem. The hour on a phone descends from a decision about trains, and it was adopted because coordination was worth more than accuracy to the sun.

Summarize how standard time came about.
questions.a: Every town once kept its own noon, which worked while travel was slow, but railway timetables could not state a departure time across many towns, so companies published their own time and stations disagreed with the towns outside them. title: The Detector a Kilometre Underground
standard_text:
Standard: By the end of the year, read and comprehend literary nonfiction at the high end of the grades 6-8 text complexity band independently and proficiently.
 Spiral: RI.8.1 citing evidence · RI.8.2 central idea · RI.8.4 word meaning · RI.8.8 claims and evidence
 Lower range: LL 870 – 970

paras.label: A
paras.text: A neutrino is a particle with almost no mass and no electric charge, and it passes through matter as though the matter were not there. Enormous numbers from the sun are going through this page and through you now.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Detecting something that barely interacts requires a great deal of material and a great deal of patience. A detector is built as a very large tank of liquid, watched by thousands of light sensors, waiting for the rare occasion when one neutrino hits a nucleus.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The difficulty is not the signal. It is everything else. Cosmic rays strike the atmosphere constantly and the particles they produce would swamp a detector at the surface, with real events lost in an enormous background.

paras.label: D
paras.text: So the detectors are put underground, in mines and under mountains. A kilometre of rock stops almost everything else while leaving neutrinos entirely unaffected, which is the one situation where being hard to stop is useful.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The first such experiment produced a famous problem. It measured neutrinos from the sun and found about a third of the number the understood physics of the sun predicted, and the shortfall persisted for three decades.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Two explanations competed. Either the model of the sun was wrong, or the neutrinos were changing on the way, into kinds the detector could not see, and settling it required a detector sensitive to all three kinds.

paras.label: G
paras.text: That experiment reported in 2001 and found the total was right. The neutrinos had been changing type in flight, which meant they have a small mass, which the existing theory of particles had said they did not.

questions.q: Why are neutrino detectors built underground?
questions.a: Cosmic rays striking the atmosphere produce particles that would swamp a detector at the surface, and a kilometre of rock stops almost everything else while leaving neutrinos unaffected.

questions.q: Paragraph E (i.e. the shortfall in solar neutrinos) and paragraph G (i.e. what the 2001 result showed).
Summarize the solar neutrino problem and how it was settled.
questions.a: Neutrinos barely interact, so detectors are enormous tanks placed a kilometre underground where rock removes the cosmic ray background. An early experiment found about a third of the neutrinos the physics of the sun predicted, and either the model was wrong or the neutrinos were changing type in flight, which a detector sensitive to all three kinds confirmed in 2001, showing they have a small mass.

questions.q:
cosmic ray: a high-energy particle arriving from space, whose products would otherwise swamp a detector.
shortfall: the gap between what was measured and what was predicted, here about two thirds of the expected neutrinos.
Describe the connection between neutrinos changing type and their having mass.
questions.a: The 2001 result showed the total was right and the neutrinos had been changing type in flight, which means they have a small mass, contrary to what the existing theory of particles had said.

note: A thirty-year disagreement where both sides were testable and one was right. Worth putting beside the RI.8.9 articles, where most disagreements are not like this.
